newsitem.title: UK: Norwegian bonds to feel pinch on drop in oil price.
newsitem.headline: Norwegian bonds to feel pinch on drop in oil price.

text.p: The Norwegian bond market's unusual liking for high oil prices leaves it exposed to the oil market's recent decline, and suggests wider yield spreads against other European markets in the near-term, analysts say.

"There could be a second round effect on sentiment on Norway which will push the spread between Norway and Bunds out...closer to 35 basis points on the 10-year position," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking (LBB).
The Norwegian/German 10-year yield spread stood at 24 basis points on Monday, compared with parity on January 10. Analysts say the drop in oil prices since the New Year is responsible for the trend.
Low oil prices are generally seen as positive for global bonds as they means inflation -- bonds' worst enemy -- is losing sway.
But oil is liquid gold for Norwegian bonds, representing 14 percent of the country's gross domestic product and substantially boosting government coffers.

The price of a barrel of benchmark Brent crude has dropped from $24.91 on January 9 to a low of $18.68 on March 3, depressed by rising supplies and a mild northern hemisphere winter. This makes the outlook for Norwegian government finances less positive.
"Oil makes up such a significant proportion of GDP," Lewis said. "It makes up an even more significant proportion of the market's perception of Norway."
Jouni Kokko, senior analyst at SE Banken in New York, sees the 10-year Norwegian-German spread widening to between 30 and 40 basis points in the short term.
Stephanie Pfeifer, European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, also forecast a widening of spreads in line with falling oil prices.

"We expect the oil price to come under further pressure after the winter...we expect a further underperformance (in Norwegian bonds), given our forecast for the oil price," she said in a note to clients.

But longer term, analysts are more bullish on Norwegian bonds because of the strong crown and benign fundamentals. Concern that some European countries may not meet the tough criteria for the launch of a single currency in January 1999 is alos positive for Norway.
"The long-term trend is towards a much narrower spread ... Norway is going to trade through Germany in the next year or so," Kokko said.
"Norway has a very good chance of becoming a real (EMU) safe haven," he added.

Norway cannot join European Economic and Monetary Union because Norwegians rejected membership of the European Union in a referendum in 1994. There are no plans to hold another referendum for at least the next several years.
Lewis noted however that the Norwegian/German spread was very volatile as it was unaffected by EMU considerations. and so moved outside the focus of the general run of global investors.
"The spread can get to levels where the vigilant investor can pick up bargains, but I wouldn't say we're at that point at the moment, we're at the other end of the spread," he said.
